lines.text: So let's go back to Isaac Newton. It's the start of sixteen sixty-six, a hundred years before Dalton is born. At least, that's the date Newton gives when he writes it up, six years later.
He's twenty-three. He has just bought a triangular glass prism. People already know a prism can throw colours on a wall.
Newton wants to know where those colours come from. So he darkens his room. He makes a small hole in his window shutter. And he lets one thin beam of sunlight in.
He puts the prism in the beam. The glass bends the light. And on the far wall, a band of colours appears. Red at one end, violet at the other, and everything in between.

The first thing that surprises him is its shape. The beam came in through a small round hole. But the band on the wall is long, about five times longer than it is wide. By the rules he'd been taught, he says, it should have been round.
At the time, most people who thought about it believed something simple. White light is pure. The prism changes it, and that's what makes the colours.
Newton suspects it's the other way round. So he sets up a test he will later call the Experimentum Crucis. The crucial experiment.
He lets the band of colours fall on a board with a small hole in it. Only one colour gets through. Say, just the blue. Then he sends that blue light through a second prism.

If the glass makes the colours, the second prism should turn that blue into something else. It doesn't. The blue bends again, by its own fixed amount. He tries the other colours too. Once a colour is separated, he says, it "obstinately retained its colour". Whatever he did to it.
So the prism isn't making the colours. It's sorting them. Every kind of ray was in the white sunlight all along, mixed together. The glass just spreads them out.
He checks it the other way, too. He gathers the spread-out rays back together with a lens. Where they meet, they make white again. In his words, light "entirely and perfectly white".
Ever seen a little rainbow thrown on a wall by a window, or a glass of water? Then you've seen the first half of his experiment.

In his letter, he puts it like this. "Colours are not Qualifications of Light, derived from Refractions, or Reflections of natural Bodies." Put simply, glass doesn't create colour. Light bouncing off things doesn't create it either. Each kind of ray carries something fixed, and that decides which colour you'll see.
He sends all this in a letter from Cambridge, in February sixteen seventy-two. It's printed in the Philosophical Transactions, the journal run by the Royal Society's secretary.
Plenty of readers like it. But not all of them. Robert Hooke, a leading London scientist, is not impressed. And says so. The arguments, with Hooke and others, drag on by letter for about six years.
But notice what Newton has done. He's taken colour out of the glass. So where is it?
